p: The king is Ptolemy IV of Egypt (221-204 BC); his Greek surname means "father-loving."
b: Ptolemy IV, called Philopator ("lover of his father"), ruled Egypt from 221 to 204 BC. His rival Antiochus is Antiochus III "the Great," the Seleucid king of Syria, who had seized the lands between the two kingdoms. The book starts abruptly: its first Greek words are "Now Philopator," as if something came before, and 2:25 speaks of companions "already mentioned" whom the book never mentions. Either an opening has been lost, or the writer expected readers to know the story. Daniel 11:10-12, which most readers take to describe these same wars, says of the "king of the south" at this point: "his heart will swell with pride" (Daniel 11:12).

p: Polybius, a Greek historian of the 100s BC, tells of the same battle near Gaza, fought on 22 June 217 BC.
b: Raphia lay on the coast road south of Gaza, at the edge of Egypt. The Greek historian Polybius describes the campaign at length (Histories 5.79-86). He says Ptolemy won with his phalanx, that Antiochus lost nearly ten thousand foot soldiers killed and four thousand captured, and that afterward the towns of Coele-Syria competed to honor the winner with crowns and sacrifices (5.86). The opening of 3 Maccabees agrees with this outline, so most scholars treat these first verses as close to history, whatever they think of what follows. The date, 22 June 217 BC, is the one modern historians give from Polybius.

p: Arsinoe III was Ptolemy's full sister and also his wife, as Ptolemaic custom allowed.
b: Arsinoe III, daughter of Ptolemy III, married her brother Ptolemy IV late in 220 BC; brother-sister marriage was a custom of the Ptolemaic royal house, borrowed from the pharaohs. The book calls her only "his sister." Polybius says that before the battle she and the king rode along the lines and addressed the troops (Histories 5.83). He does not describe her loosened hair or tears, or the promise of gold that 1:4 gives her; those details are the book's own, or come from a source now lost.

p: Polybius tells the same raid: Theodotus, a deserter from Ptolemy, missed the king and killed his doctor.
b: Theodotus the Aetolian had served Ptolemy and gone over to Antiochus. Polybius tells how he slipped into Ptolemy's camp before dawn with two companions and searched the tent where the king worked and dined; but the king slept in another tent, so Theodotus wounded two men, killed the king's physician Andreas, and got away (Histories 5.81). Polybius blames Theodotus for not finding out where the king slept. 3 Maccabees tells it differently: the king was saved because a Jew, Dositheus, moved him and put a stand-in in his bed (1:3). The two accounts agree that the king was not where the killer looked.

p: The man who saves the king's life is a Jew who has given up the law. The book makes nothing of his help.
b: Dositheus, "called Drimylus's son," is a Jew by birth who "changed the customs" (Greek metabalōn ta nomima) and became estranged from "the teachings of his fathers." He appears only here. Polybius, telling the same night raid, does not name him (Histories 5.81). The writer could have used him to show Jewish loyalty to the crown, which 3:3 and 3:21 stress, but instead marks him as an apostate and drops him. The book's later bargain, citizenship for those who give up the law (2:30-33), and the killing of apostates in 7:10-15, show how seriously it takes that line.

p: A mina was a weight of a hundred drachmas; two minas of gold was a fortune for a soldier.
b: The mina was a Greek unit of weight and money, equal to a hundred drachmas, and the sum here is in gold, not silver. Two minas of gold for every man was a promise far beyond a soldier's pay. Compare the reward of two thousand drachmas that the king offers informers in 3:28.

a: he handed out gifts to their shrines
p: Ptolemy honors the gods of the cities he has won; this sets up his visit to Jerusalem.
b: The Greek word is temenos, a sacred precinct around a temple. Hellenistic kings bought the loyalty of conquered cities by endowing their gods. Polybius says the towns of Coele-Syria honored Ptolemy with crowns and sacrifices after Raphia (Histories 5.86), and the "Raphia Decree" of 15 November 217 BC honored the king after the victory. So the king's visit to Jerusalem is meant to look like one more stop on a tour of thanks. In his own letter he boasts of it (3:16).

p: The gerousia, the governing council of the Jews in Jerusalem under the Greek kings.
b: Greek gerousia, from gerōn, "old man": the council of elders that governed the Jews of Judea in the Greek period, beside the high priest. The term appears in 1 Maccabees 12:6 and 2 Maccabees 1:10; 11:27, and later its place was taken by the Sanhedrin. Here the book adds "and from the elders," perhaps meaning the leading men of the city beyond the council.

t: A king at the sanctuary: 3 Maccabees and 2 Maccabees 3
p: The story of 1:8-2:24 runs close to the story of Heliodorus in 2 Maccabees 3. Here is how they compare.
b:
In 2 Maccabees 3 a Seleucid minister, Heliodorus, comes to take the temple treasure. The priests throw themselves down "in their priestly robes" (2 Maccabees 3:15), the unmarried girls "who were usually kept shut in" run out (2 Maccabees 3:19), the people pray, and God strikes him down: two young men "flogged him" until he fell and was carried out helpless (2 Maccabees 3:26-28). 3 Maccabees has every one of these steps (1:16-2:23), even the flogging (2:21).

The differences matter. Heliodorus wants money; Ptolemy wants to see the inner room. Heliodorus is saved by the high priest's sacrifice and confesses God (2 Maccabees 3:35-36); Ptolemy recovers and "felt no regret at all" (2:24), which drives the rest of the book. Most scholars think 3 Maccabees borrowed the pattern from 2 Maccabees or from a shared tradition.

p: The book keeps two words apart: hieron, the whole temple, and naos, the holy house the king wants to enter.
b: Hieron ("the temple") is the whole sacred complex with its courts, where Ptolemy has already sacrificed. Naos ("the sanctuary") is the holy building itself. The answer in 1:11 shows what the king is after: the room only the high priest enters once a year, the Most Holy Place behind the veil. The Gospels use the same two words, and it is "the curtain of the sanctuary" that splits in two (Matthew 27:51).

a: only the high priest, who leads them all, and he only one time each year
t: Once a year, the high priest alone
p: The rule of Leviticus 16, the Day of Atonement, also known to the Mishnah and to Hebrews.
b: Leviticus 16 allows Aaron into "the holy place behind the veil" only on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:2, 34). Hebrews states the same rule: "The second tent, though, is entered by the high priest alone, once a year" (Hebrews 9:7). The Mishnah ranks the zones of holiness: Gentiles may not pass the barrier around the inner courts, and "only the high priest, on Yom Kippur, at the time of the service" may enter the Holy of Holies (Mishnah Kelim 1:8-9). Ptolemy's demand breaks the strictest boundary in Israel's worship.
r: Leviticus 16:2; Leviticus 16:34; Hebrews 9:7; Numbers 18:7; Mishnah Kelim 1:8-9

t: Uzziah, the king who went in
p: Another king once forced his way into the sanctuary and was struck there: Uzziah of Judah.
b: 2 Chronicles tells how King Uzziah, once he was strong, "went into the LORD's temple to burn incense" (2 Chronicles 26:16). The priests told him, "it is not your place" (2 Chronicles 26:18), and as he raged, skin disease broke out on his forehead and "the LORD had struck him" (2 Chronicles 26:20). Both stories have the same shape: a proud king, priests who read him the rule, and a blow from God in the holy place itself. 3 Maccabees does not name Uzziah, but Jewish readers knew the pattern.

a: to make a wonder of that very thing
p: The Greek verb means to tell of marvels or put on a show; the exact point of the reply is unclear.
b: Terateuesthai comes from teras, "wonder, portent." It can mean to talk of marvels, to boast, or to make a show of something. The reply seems to mean that the king should not boast of having entered other temples, or that doing so was itself no marvel to be proud of. Brenton (1844) has "That he did wrong to boast of this." The word "without thinking" suggests the speaker was rash to answer the king at all.

p: The book's favorite title for God, a Greek superlative also found in 2 Maccabees.
b: Ho megistos theos, literally "the greatest God," is the book's stock name for the God of Israel (here; 3:11, and often in chapters 4-7). The title claims for Israel's God the top place, in the Greek of the nations. 2 Maccabees uses it once, when Heliodorus reports "the works of the greatest God" (2 Maccabees 3:36). At 1:9 Codex Venetus has it where Alexandrinus says "the faithful God" (see the variant there), and here Venetus has "the great God."

a: Unmarried girls, who were kept shut in their rooms
p: Well-born girls were kept at home until marriage; that they run into the street shows the panic.
b: Greek katakleistoi parthenoi, "virgins shut in." In Greek and Jewish cities of the time, unmarried daughters of good families stayed indoors and out of public view (compare Sirach 42:11, which tells a father to keep strict watch over a headstrong daughter). 2 Maccabees uses the same picture for Heliodorus's visit: "the unmarried girls, who were usually kept shut in" ran to the gates and walls (2 Maccabees 3:19). Both writers use the broken custom to show a city turned upside down.

p: Throwing dust on the head was a sign of grief and pleading, as in Joshua and Lamentations.
b: When Israel was beaten at Ai, Joshua and the elders "threw dust on their heads" (Joshua 7:6). In Lamentations, after Jerusalem fell, "Dust is on their heads; sackcloth is tied around them" (Lamentations 2:10). The gesture says: we are brought low to the ground, have pity on us. Here it is done before the disaster, as a plea to stop it.

p: A rare, piled-up Greek word: "the all-highest temple."
b: Panypertatos joins "all" (pan-), "over" (hyper) and a superlative ending: "above everything, highest of all." Brenton rendered it "the Most High temple." The writer loves such inflated words, the style of Greek rhetoric of his day; the Plain keeps the sense in simpler words.

a: They called for a rush to arms
p: Some young men want to fight, but the elders bring them back to prayer. The book sides with the elders.
b: In 1 Maccabees, zeal for the law leads to armed revolt (1 Maccabees 2:27-28), and the Hasmoneans decide to fight even on the Sabbath (1 Maccabees 2:41). 3 Maccabees tells a different story: the bold citizens who call for arms are "turned back" to prayer, and it is prayer, not swords, that saves the temple (2:21). The same is true later in Egypt, where the Jews have no army and are saved by Eleazar's prayer (6:1-15). Readers who date the book to the Roman period see in this a lesson for a minority that could not rebel; others read it simply as faith in God's rescue.

p: The narrator writes as a Jew: "our people." And even the king's own men pray to Israel's God.
b: Greek syn tois hēmeterois, "with ours." The writer speaks as one of the Jewish community and assumes Jewish readers. The scene is striking: the king's Greek officers join the Jews in calling on "the one who holds every power." Jonah's sailors do the same when the storm hits (Jonah 1:14). In this book the Gentiles who matter are sometimes friends (3:8-10), not only enemies.

a: the walls and the whole floor echoed too
p: Creation itself seems to protest: the walls and floor join the cry.
b: The image of stones and walls that cry out appears in Habakkuk: "For the stone in the wall cries out, / and the wooden beam answers it" (Habakkuk 2:11). Jesus uses it at his entry to Jerusalem: "if these fall silent, the stones will shout it out" (Luke 19:40). The writer says only that it "seemed" so, but the effect is that the temple building itself refuses the outrage.

p: Most readers identify him with Simon II, the high priest praised in Sirach 50.
b: Readers and scholars identify him as Simon II, the high priest whom Sirach praises at length: "Simon son of Onias, the great priest, who in his life repaired the house" (Sirach 50:1, from the Greek). 2 Maccabees 3 makes his son Onias III the hero of the Heliodorus story. Jewish tradition also tells of a high priest Simon, "Shimon HaTzaddik" (Simon the Righteous), who went out in his robes to meet Alexander the Great and saved the temple (Bavli Yoma 69a). Which Simon that story means is debated.

p: Simon prays as Solomon did at the temple's dedication: on his knees, hands spread out.
b: When Solomon dedicated the temple he "lifted his open palms to the heavens" (1 Kings 8:22) and prayed "down on his knees, with his palms spread toward the heavens" (1 Kings 8:54). Simon's prayer that follows leans on Solomon's: God chose this place for his name and promised to hear prayer made there (2:9-10). Ezra prays the same way (Ezra 9:5).

a: Lord, Lord, King of the heavens and Master of all creation
p: Simon piles up titles for God, in the style of Greek-speaking Jewish prayer.
b: Each title has a Greek word behind it: Kyrie "Lord" (the Greek books have no divine name, so not "the LORD"), basileu tōn ouranōn "King of the heavens," despota "Master," hagie en hagiois "Holy One among the holy," monarche "only Ruler," and pantokratōr "Almighty." The prayers of 2 Maccabees open in the same way (2 Maccabees 1:24-25). The titles do work: a God who rules all creation can rule one proud king.
orig: Κύριε, Κύριε, βασιλεῦ τῶν οὐρανῶν, καὶ δέσποτα πάσης τῆς κτίσεως

a: who snorts with boldness and strength
p: The verb is used of a spirited horse; Psalm 2 uses it of the nations that rage against God.
b: Phryassomai means to snort and toss the head like a horse, so to be haughty. The Greek of Psalm 2:1 uses the same verb: "Why did the nations rage" (Acts 4:25, where the church quotes it under persecution). Simon's choice of word sets Ptolemy among the rulers of Psalm 2 who rise against the Lord.

p: Following the Greek of Genesis 6:4, Simon blames the giants for the wrong that brought the Flood.
b: Where the Hebrew of Genesis 6:4 has "the Nephilim," the Septuagint says gigantes, "giants." Jewish writers of this period told much of them: 1 Enoch says the Watchers' wives "gave birth to huge giants" (1 Enoch 7:2). A similar list of warnings, the giants, Lot's neighbors, and the six hundred thousand who hardened their hearts in the wilderness, appears in the Greek of Sirach 16:7-10, and Wisdom remembers the Flood "when the proud giants were dying" (Wisdom 14:6). Genesis itself blames human violence in general (Genesis 6:11-13). Simon's prayer joins a common Jewish way of reading Genesis, not something new.
r: Genesis 6:4; Genesis 6:11-13; Sirach 16:7-10; Wisdom 14:6; 1 Enoch 7:1-6; 2 Peter 2:4-5

p: Simon names Sodom's sin as arrogance, as Ezekiel does; other passages stress violence and sexual sin.
b: Genesis 19 tells of the men of Sodom who tried to rape Lot's guests. Ezekiel names the root: "Here is the guilt of Sodom, your sister: pride" (Ezekiel 16:49). Jude stresses that they "went after other flesh" (Jude 7). Simon's prayer picks pride because the prayer is about a proud king: the word comes back in 2:3, 2:17 and 2:21. Like 2 Peter, it makes Sodom a lesson: God set them "up as an example for those who would be ungodly later" (2 Peter 2:6).

a: you drowned him under the deep sea
p: Simon retells the crossing of the Sea of Reeds from Exodus 14-15.
b: In Exodus, "The waters came back and covered the chariots and the horsemen, all Pharaoh's army" (Exodus 14:28), and then "Moses and the Israelites sang this song to the LORD" (Exodus 15:1), as 2:8 says: "they praised you." Pharaoh's "testing" with plagues (2:6) and his drowning give the pattern for the whole book: a king who enslaves God's people, a rescue, and a song. In 6:4 the priest Eleazar will use the same example.

p: Simon builds on Deuteronomy's "place the LORD will choose" and Solomon's prayer.
b: Deuteronomy tells Israel to seek "the place the LORD your God will choose out of all your tribes to put his name there" (Deuteronomy 12:5). Solomon's dedication prayer asks God to keep his eyes on the house where he said, "My name will be there" (1 Kings 8:29). Simon adds a Greek thought: God "lacks nothing." A later Jewish prayer says the same: "You, Lord of all things, who lack nothing, chose with pleasure to have a temple" (2 Maccabees 14:35), and Paul tells the Athenians that God is not served "as if he were short of anything" (Acts 17:25).

p: Epiphaneia: a visible showing of God's power, the favorite word of 2 Maccabees.
b: Epiphaneia means an appearance or manifestation, especially a god's visible help. Here it recalls the glory that filled Solomon's temple at its dedication (1 Kings 8:10-11; 2 Chronicles 7:1-3). 2 Maccabees uses the word for God's interventions (2 Maccabees 3:24), and 3 Maccabees uses the noun again for the rescue at the hippodrome (5:8, 51), and the verb in 6:9 and 6:18. The same word gave the Christian feast of Epiphany its name.

p: Simon reminds God of the promise in Solomon's prayer: when Israel turns back and prays at the temple, God will hear.
b: Solomon asked: if the people sin and are defeated, then turn back and pray "in this house," hear and forgive (1 Kings 8:33-34). God answered that if his people humble themselves and pray, "I myself will hear from the heavens" (2 Chronicles 7:14). King Jehoshaphat used the promise in a crisis: "Out of our trouble we will cry to you, and you will hear and save" (2 Chronicles 20:9). Simon does the same. The Bible's words are a request in Solomon's mouth; Simon takes them as a promise.

p: The pair of words describes God in Deuteronomy's Greek and Christ in Revelation.
b: The Greek of Deuteronomy 32:4 calls God "faithful" (pistos) and his works "true" (alēthina). Revelation gives the pair to Christ as a name: "The one riding it is called Faithful and True" (Revelation 19:11; compare Revelation 3:14). Here it is the ground of the prayer: God will keep the promise just recalled.

a: because of our many great sins
p: Simon confesses the people's sins, although the outrage is the king's, not theirs.
b: The prayer follows the pattern of Israel's prayers after the exile: we have sinned, so we are under our enemies (Nehemiah 9:33-37; Daniel 9:5-16). In this story, though, the Jews have done nothing wrong; the book stresses their loyalty (3:3-5). Some readers see a humble confession that all Israel needs mercy; others see a tension in the book between this old explanation of suffering and its newer picture of innocent people persecuted for their faith, closer to Daniel 3 and 6. 2 Maccabees holds both together: the punishments are "meant, not for ruin, but for the correction of our people" (2 Maccabees 6:12).

p: The phrase comes from Solomon's prayer in the Greek: God's home is beyond all heavens, yet he chose a house on earth.
b: In the Greek of 1 Kings 8:27 Solomon says that "the heaven and the heaven of heaven" cannot hold God (the site's Plain, from the Hebrew: "the heavens, the heavens above the heavens, are not big enough for you"). Simon makes the same two-sided point in 2:15-16: God lives where no human can reach, yet he chose to put his glory in this place. That is why its profaning matters. Isaiah 66:1 asks the question from the other side: "Where then is the house that you would build for me?"

a: Do not punish us through these men's uncleanness
p: The Greek "in" could mean "by means of" these men, or "for" their uncleanness. The first fits best.
b: The Greek preposition en can mean "in, by means of" or loosely "because of." Simon is not asking God to excuse Israel for the Gentiles' sin. He asks God not to use these unclean men as his tool to punish his people, as Habakkuk complained that God used the Babylonians (Habakkuk 1:12-13). Brenton has "by means of."
orig: μὴ ἐκδικήσῃς ἡμᾶς ἐν τῇ τούτων ἀκαθαρσίᾳ

a: We have trampled the house of holiness
p: The boast Simon fears is a lament heard often in Israel's Scriptures: the foe tramples the holy place.
b: Isaiah laments, "our foes have trampled your sanctuary" (Isaiah 63:18). Daniel's vision asks how long the holy place will be "trampled" (Daniel 8:13), and 1 Maccabees mourns, "Your holy place is trampled and profaned" (1 Maccabees 3:51). Jesus speaks of Jerusalem "trampled" by the nations (Luke 21:24), and Revelation of the holy city trampled for forty-two months (Revelation 11:2). The "loathsome idols" are prosochthismata, a Septuagint word for idols as things God loathes.

p: The verb of David's prayer in Psalm 51, in the Greek: wipe sins away like writing from a page.
b: Apaleiphō means to wipe off, as ink from a page. Psalm 51 asks God to "wipe out my rebellions" (Psalm 51:1), and Isaiah hears God say, "I myself, I am the one / who wipes away your rebellions" (Isaiah 43:25). Simon prays in the words of Israel's own Scripture.

a: Let your compassion come quickly to meet us
p: Simon quotes the Greek of Psalm 79:8, a lament over a temple defiled by the nations.
b: The Greek words are those of Psalm 78:8 in the Septuagint (Psalm 79:8 in English Bibles): tachy prokatalabetōsan ... hoi oiktirmoi sou. The site's Plain renders that verse from the Hebrew: "Hurry, let your compassion come out to meet us" (Psalm 79:8). The choice is apt, for Psalm 79 begins: "God, the nations have come in, into your inheritance. / They have made your holy temple unclean" (Psalm 79:1). The closing words echo Psalm 34:18: "he saves those whose spirits are crushed."

p: A rare title for God: propatōr, "forefather." Paul uses the word of Abraham.
b: Propatōr means a first ancestor. Paul uses it of Abraham, "our forefather according to the flesh" (Romans 4:1). Calling God the forefather of Israel is unusual; it may mean the first Father of all things, or the Father of the nation (compare Deuteronomy 32:6; Isaiah 63:16). Brenton found the phrase hard and wrote "who is beyond all Holy among the holy." The prayer is called enthesmos, "lawful": offered as it should be, by the right person in the right place.

p: The answer to prayer is a blow from God, as with Heliodorus and later Herod. The 66 books tell such stories too.
b: Heliodorus was "flogged from heaven" (2 Maccabees 3:34) by two young men; here God himself does the flogging, with no angel named. The 66 books have their own stories of proud rulers struck by God: Uzziah in the temple (2 Chronicles 26:20), Nebuchadnezzar driven out to the fields (Daniel 4:31-33), and Herod Agrippa, whom "an angel of the Lord struck" because he took God's glory (Acts 12:23). 3 Maccabees agrees with them that God defends his honor; it goes beyond them in telling of a blow to a king of Egypt that no other ancient source records.

a: like a reed in the wind
p: The image of weakness Jesus later uses of the people's expectations about John the Baptist.
b: A reed bends whichever way the wind pushes it. Jesus asks the crowds about John: "what did you go to gaze at? A reed that the wind shakes?" (Matthew 11:7). Here the mighty king is the reed, shaken this way and that by God. Compare the bruised reed of Isaiah 42:3, which God's servant will not break.

p: "Friend" was a court rank at the Hellenistic courts, as in 1 and 2 Maccabees.
b: The philoi were the king's inner circle, a formal rank at the Ptolemaic and Seleucid courts. The site writes it with a capital, as in 1 Maccabees and 2 Maccabees ("one of the king's Friends"). At 2:26 many of these Friends follow the king's will against the Jews.

a: he felt no regret at all
t: A heart that does not change
p: Unlike Heliodorus, Ptolemy learns nothing. His hardness drives the rest of the book.
b: Heliodorus, once struck, sacrifices to God and tells everyone of his power (2 Maccabees 3:35-36). Ptolemy goes home "making bitter threats." Readers have long compared him with Pharaoh, who, when the hail stopped, "sinned once more. He made his heart heavy" (Exodus 9:34). He changes only later, after God puts "a forgetting" into his mind (5:28) and at last turns his anger into pity (6:22). The Greek metamelos means "regret, change of mind"; Matthew uses the related verb when Judas "regretted it" (Matthew 27:3).

p: No drinking companions have been mentioned in the book as we have it.
b: The Greek proapodedeigmenōn means "previously pointed out" or "appointed before." The book has not named any drinking partners. Either the phrase means "previously appointed" (his long-time favorites), or something has dropped out of the book's opening (see the note on 1:1). The king's drinking returns in chapter 5 (5:16).

a: he made slanders in those places
p: Dysphēmia means words of ill omen: slander, or even blasphemy.
b: Dysphēmia is the opposite of euphēmia, holy silence or speaking well. It can mean slander of people or blasphemy against the gods. "In those places" is vague: in Egypt, perhaps in the Jews' own places of prayer. Brenton has "he raised evil reports there." The verse explains the next one: the king's talk prepares a public decree.

a: he put up a stone pillar
p: Royal decrees were published on stone slabs set up in public; the book imagines one in Alexandria's palace quarter.
b: A stēlē was an upright stone slab carved with a text. Ptolemaic decrees were set up this way: the Raphia Decree of 15 November 217 BC, which honored this king after his victory, survives in three copies. Esther shows the same practice in Persia: a copy of the order "was to be given out as law in each province and shown openly to all the peoples" (Esther 8:13). "The tower beside the palace courtyard" places it in the royal quarter of Alexandria.

a: No one who does not sacrifice may enter their temples
p: "Their" may mean the Jews' own places of worship, or the temples of Alexandria.
b: Greek epi ta hiera autōn, "into their sacred places." If "their" means the Jews, the decree bars from the Jews' own houses of prayer anyone who will not sacrifice to the king's gods; Brenton takes it so ("their own temple"). If it means the pagan temples, the decree simply makes sacrifice the price of public religious life. Either way it forces a choice between the city's gods and Israel's God, as Daniel 3 did with the golden statue.
orig: ἐπὶ τὰ ἱερὰ αὐτῶν (epi ta hiera autōn)

p: A count of the people for a poll tax; to be on it marked you as a native subject, not a citizen.
b: Laographia, literally "people-writing," was the register of those who paid a head tax. Here it is joined to "the condition of household slaves," so the writer treats being listed as a loss of standing. Scholars who date the book to the early Roman period, such as Moses Hadas and Victor Tcherikover, point to the Roman census in Egypt of 24 BC as the event behind this verse; others think a Ptolemaic census could also fit. Luke's "the whole inhabited world was to be registered" (Luke 2:1) uses the related verb apographō, as 2:29 and 2:32 do.

a: the mark of Dionysus, an ivy leaf
p: Ptolemy IV was devoted to Dionysus, god of wine and of the mysteries; the ivy was his plant.
b: Ivy was sacred to Dionysus (Bacchus), and his worshipers wore and carried it, as in 2 Maccabees: "they were made to march in Dionysus's parade carrying ivy" (2 Maccabees 6:7). Ptolemy IV made much of the god and linked him closely to the royal cult, and sometime before 217 BC he ordered all priests of Dionysus to come to Alexandria to be registered. The book turns that history into a threat: Jews who are registered must wear the god's mark.

p: The law forbade marks on the skin; Revelation's "mark" is a word from the same root as the verb here.
b: The verb is charassesthai, "to be engraved, branded." The noun from the same root, charagma, is the "mark" of the beast that everyone must take "on their right hand or on their forehead" (Revelation 13:16). Slaves were branded in the ancient world, so the mark also says "owned." The law of Moses forbade it: "do not put tattooed writing on yourselves. I am the LORD" (Leviticus 19:28). Paul, by contrast, says he carries "the marks of Jesus" in his body (Galatians 6:17), using another word.

a: under the reduced rights already set for them
p: A hard phrase: perhaps the lower legal standing set out earlier for the Jews.
b: The Greek eis tēn prosynestalmenēn authentian is obscure: authentia means "authority" or "status," and the participle means "restricted beforehand." It seems to mean that the registered Jews would be entered on the rolls with the lesser standing already decreed in 2:28. Brenton has "set apart with these limited rights." Venetus reads "to be registered" without "beforehand."
orig: οὓς καὶ προκαταχωρίσαι εἰς τὴν προσυνεσταλμένην αὐθεντίαν

p: Jews who join the mysteries of Dionysus may become equal citizens. The offer is the book's real test.
b: Teletai were the secret initiation rites of mystery cults; Dionysus's were among the most popular. The king offers what many Alexandrian Jews wanted, equal standing with the Greek citizens of the city, at the price of their faith. The historian Victor Tcherikover noted that initiation into this cult was a status symbol that people had to petition for. For the writer, a Jew who buys citizenship this way has left the people of God (2:33).
orig: ἐν τοῖς κατὰ τελετὰς μεμυημένοις (en tois kata teletas memyēmenois)

p: Isopolitai: people with the same civic rights. The Jews' legal standing in Alexandria was a burning question.
b: Isopolitēs means one who has equal citizen rights. Alexandria's Jews lived as an organized community with their own laws, but whether they also held the citizenship of the Greek city was disputed, and the dispute turned violent in the Roman period. The book's view is plain: citizenship is good when offered fairly (3:21, where the king boasts of offering it), but not at the cost of the law. The word politeia, "citizenship" (3:21, 23), is the same word that 2 Maccabees uses for a people's "way of life."

a: the steps that the city's godliness required
p: A hard phrase. Epibathra means a step, ladder or gangplank; the sense seems to be the price of faithfulness.
b: Literally "hating the steps of the city's godliness" (tas tēs poleōs eusebeias epibathras). Epibathra is a step up or a boarding plank, so the phrase may mean the hard climb that faithfulness asked of the community, or the price of entry into the faith of their city, Jerusalem. Venetus first wrote "over the city" (epi poleōs) instead of "lightly," and Brenton has "those who were over the city." Whichever is right, the point is clear: some Jews found their faith a burden and traded it for status.

a: They loathed those of their own who went over
p: The faithful cut off those who went over to the king. The book returns to them at its end.
b: The faithful Jews treat the converts as "enemies of the nation" and shut them out of shared life and mutual help. The book approves, and at the end it has the king allow the faithful to kill such apostates (7:10-15, see the notes there). Jewish and Christian readers alike have judged that ending harshly. The Bible itself has rules for excluding the unfaithful from the community (Ezra 10:8; 1 Corinthians 5:11), but the line from exclusion to violence is the hard question this book raises.

a: the Jews out in the country
p: Ptolemaic Egypt was divided between Alexandria, a Greek city, and the countryside along the Nile, the chōra.
b: Greek tois en tē chōra, "those in the country." In Ptolemaic Egypt the chōra meant all the land outside Alexandria and the few Greek cities: the villages and towns of the Nile valley, where many Jews served as soldiers, farmers and officials. The king's anger now spreads from the capital to every Jew in the land, as in Esther the decree goes "to every province of the king" (Esther 3:13).
orig: τοῖς ἐν τῇ χώρᾳ (tois en tē chōra)

a: the Jews kept them from their customs
t: What were the Jews accused of?
p: The charge is hard to pin down in the Greek: perhaps that Jews hindered others' customs, or kept apart from them.
b: The Greek hōs an apo tōn nomimōn autous kōlyontōn says "as if they were hindering them from the customs." It may mean the Jews were blamed for keeping others from the city's religious customs, or for standing in the way of the king's laws. Brenton has "the Jews kept them away from the ordinances of the law." Verses 4-7 make the real issue clear: Jewish separateness in worship and food.
orig: ὡς ἂν ἀπὸ τῶν νομίμων αὐτοὺς κωλυόντων

a: they kept themselves apart in the matter of food
p: The food laws set the Jews apart, and their neighbors resented it, as Haman says in Esther.
b: The laws of clean and unclean food (Leviticus 11; Deuteronomy 14) meant that Jews could not share most pagan meals or sacrifices. Daniel "set his heart on not defiling himself with the king's rich food" (Daniel 1:8). Haman's charge to the Persian king is the same as here: "Their laws are unlike any other people's, and the king's laws they do not obey" (Esther 3:8). The writer admits the separation and defends it: they kept apart in food, but were just and well liked in everything else (3:5).

p: Allophyloi: the book's word for the hostile non-Jews, set apart from the friendly "Greeks in the city" (3:8).
b: Allophyloi, "those of another tribe," is the Septuagint's word for the Philistines and for foreigners. The writer uses it of the enemies of the Jews in Egypt, but he is careful to add that "the Greeks in the city" had suffered no wrong and tried to help (3:8-10). Not all Gentiles are enemies in this book; the hostile ones are a group set on harm.

a: share the drink offerings of alliance
p: Greek homospondoi: people who pour a drink offering together when they make a treaty.
b: Treaties in the Greek world were sealed by pouring a libation to the gods together (spondē), so homospondos meant "ally." The accusation has two edges: the Jews are not loyal allies, and they will not join in the gods' rites that sealed every alliance. The book answers both: they are loyal (3:3), but they will not worship other gods.

p: The Greeks of Alexandria pity the Jews but dare not help; the writer calls the king's rule a tyranny.
b: In Greek political thought a tyrant was a ruler who governs by fear and for himself. The writer, who calls the king "impious" (3:1), puts that word on his rule. He also makes a point about his Greek neighbors: they knew the Jews had done no wrong, comforted them, and expected things to change. Some even pledged secret help (3:10). The book is not against Greeks; it is against a king who makes himself a god's servant against God's people.

a: a community that large, guilty of nothing
p: The Greek can mean the Greeks believed "so large a community, guilty of nothing" would not be neglected, or that "the One who knows everything" would not neglect it.
b: Mēden ēgnoēkos can mean "having done nothing wrong" (agnoeō, "to sin unknowingly") or "having been ignorant of nothing." The Plain takes it with "community": a large, innocent people would not be left alone. Brenton took it of God: "He who knoweth all things, will not ... disregard so great a people." On that reading the Greeks of the city voice a hope in providence.
orig: μὴ γὰρ οὕτω παροραθήσεσθαι τηλικοῦτο σύστεμα μηδὲν ἠγνοηκός

a: he wrote the following letter aimed at them
p: The letter of 3:12-29 closely resembles the king's letter against the Jews in the Greek Esther (Addition B).
b: The Greek Esther includes the text of the Persian king's decree (Addition B, at Esther 3:13 on this site): one hostile people, scattered among the nations, follows strange laws and ignores royal orders, so all are to be destroyed with wives and children. Ptolemy's letter makes the same charges and orders the same fate (3:19, 25). In both books a second letter later reverses the first (Esther's Addition E at 8:12; 3 Maccabees 7:1-9), and a yearly feast follows. The two books may be drawing on each other or on a shared pattern.

p: The strategoi were the governors of Egypt's districts, as well as army commanders.
b: In Ptolemaic Egypt the stratēgos was the governor of a district (a nome), in charge of order and justice there, though the word also means "general." The site renders it "governor" or "general" by context; a letter to the districts fits governors. The greeting "greetings and good health" (chairein kai errōsthai, as in 7:1) is the normal opening of a Greek letter, followed by a wish for health (3:13), as in 2 Maccabees 9:19-20.

a: In word they welcomed our coming, but in deed they were false
p: The letter retells chapters 1-2 from the king's point of view, leaving out his own humiliation.
b: In the king's version he came only to honor the temple with gifts, was falsely welcomed, and spared the Jews out of kindness. He says nothing of being struck down. The reader, who has just seen it, knows the letter is self-serving, and the gap is the writer's irony. The same device runs through Esther, where Haman's words to the king hide what he intends (Esther 3:8-9).

p: The charge that Jews set themselves against everyone was a common slander in the ancient world.
b: The letter accuses the Jews of being the only people who hold their heads high against kings. Haman's charge in Esther is similar (Esther 3:8), and the Greek Esther's royal letter calls them "one hostile people" among all nations. The writer lets the charge stand in the king's mouth, so that the reader can measure it against what he has already said: the Jews were loyal and well thought of by everyone (3:3-5).

p: The king claims he offered the Jews full citizenship of Alexandria, the honor they most wanted.
b: The king boasts that he wanted to raise the Jews to politeia, the citizenship of the Greek city, and blames them for refusing. The reader knows the hidden price from 2:30: initiation into the king's cult. "Their kin here" are the Jews of Egypt, kin to those of Jerusalem; "their service as allies" likely recalls the Jewish soldiers who had long served the Ptolemies.

p: To a Greek king, a barbaros was anyone who did not speak Greek or live as a Greek.
b: Barbaros first meant someone whose speech sounds like "bar-bar," a non-Greek. The king calls Greek-speaking Jews of Alexandria "barbarians," denying them a place in Greek civilization. 2 Maccabees turns the word around, saying the Jewish fighters "drove the barbarian crowds before them" (2 Maccabees 2:21), and Paul uses it simply of non-Greek speakers (Romans 1:14).

p: The verb means to beat on the tympanon, a frame used for torture. Hebrews uses the same word of the martyrs.
b: Apotympanizō comes from tympanon, a drum, here a wooden frame on which a victim was stretched and beaten. Eleazar in 2 Maccabees "walked toward the torture frame" (2 Maccabees 6:19), and Hebrews remembers that "others were tortured on the rack" (Hebrews 11:35), with the verb tympanizō. The threat falls on any Gentile who hides a Jew, which is just what the friendly neighbors of 3:10 had promised to do.

t: From the old to the infant
p: The decree, like Haman's, spares no one, "from the young to the old, little children and women" (Esther 3:13).
b: Esther's decree orders the Jews killed "from the young to the old, little children and women, all in one day" (Esther 3:13). Ptolemy's letter goes further by threatening the Gentiles who shelter them. Pharaoh's order against Hebrew babies (Exodus 1:22) is the oldest pattern behind both.

p: A slave who informs will be freed. Royal decrees often paid informers with part of the guilty person's goods.
b: "Crowned with freedom" means the informer, if a slave, will be set free, with the crown as a public honor. The informer also gets the property of the person he reports and two thousand drachmas, a large sum (see 1:4 on money). The writer means the reader to feel how such a decree would turn neighbors and household servants against each other.

a: that place is to be put off-limits and set on fire
p: Persian decrees in Ezra and Daniel end with the same kind of threat against a guilty house.
b: Royal decrees in the Bible end with threats like this. Darius orders that a man who changes his decree be impaled and "His house is to be made a dunghill for this" (Ezra 6:11); Nebuchadnezzar says that anyone who speaks against Israel's God will be hacked apart "and its house will be made a dunghill" (Daniel 3:29). The Greek Esther's second royal letter ends with the same sort of threat against any city that disobeys. Here the threat is turned against those who protect the Jews.
